extracted.intended_audience: general readers and TV history/ comedy enthusiasts
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive documentation and historical summary of a 1950s live American 90-minute variety/sketch-comedy television program, its production, performers, sketches, preservation, and reception. Useful for readers researching the show's features, influence, and archival status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live 90-minute weekly broadcast format and performance discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Your Show of Shows is a live 90-minute variety show broadcast weekly on NBC from 1950–1954.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes the demands of live television: performers had "no cue cards, no TelePrompTers, and no ad-libbing on the air" and "Nobody ever forgot a line," illustrating a high level of rehearsal and discipline required for live broadcasts. Production locations (International Theatre, Center Theatre) and the multi-camera setup are noted as part of the format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing quality and comedic voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The series featured "superbly written sketches that poked fun at human foibles and pretensions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers included Mel Brooks, Neil Simon, Mel Tolkin, Lucille Kallen, Selma Diamond, Joseph Stein, Michael Stewart, Tony Webster, and Carl Reiner (who also acted). The page treats the strength and roster of writers as central to the show's excellence and comedic style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation in variety format (narrative elements / sitcom integration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically significant for evolving the variety genre by incorporating situation comedies such as the running sketch 'The Hickenloopers', adding narrative elements to the traditional multi-act structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This blending of sketch and recurring-character sitcom elements is cited as an innovative structural contribution and a criterion by which the show's influence is assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast performance and chemistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Featured performers Sid Caesar, Imogene Coca, Carl Reiner, Howard Morris, and others whose onstage personae (Everyman, torch singer, daffy ballerina, the Hickenloopers) created comedic variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page highlights the 'special chemistry' between Caesar and Coca and examples of character types and recurring pairings (e.g., Doris and Charlie Hickenlooper) as key to audience appeal and comic effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production leadership, direction, and choreography
rubrics_metrics.description: Produced by Sylvester 'Pat' Weaver and directed/produced by Max Liebman; James Starbuck was resident choreographer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Max Liebman's production style (willingness to throw out material at the last minute, strictness about ad-libbing) and the inclusion of choreography and musical direction are presented as essential production standards that shaped the show's quality and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring musical sketches and variety content mix
rubrics_metrics.description: The show featured regular musical sketches (e.g., the mock rock group The Three Haircuts) and an array of glamorous dancers alongside comedy sketches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The balance of musical numbers, dance parodies, and sketch comedy (including parodies of ballets and vocal trios) is treated as a defining characteristic of the show's variety format and entertainment value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archival preservation and survivability
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the series has been preserved to some extent (kinescopes retained by Max Liebman); Paley Center holds an almost complete set; master tapes of the 1976 syndicated series exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preservation is discussed as important for historical access: a 1973 theatrical compilation (Ten from Your Show of Shows), a 1976 syndicated 'best of' series, discovery of original scripts in 2000, and availability of some sketches on DVD are given as evidence of archival survival and public availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural influence and legacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The series inspired later works (e.g., The Dick Van Dyke Show, the movie My Favorite Year, and Neil Simon's play Laughter on the 23rd Floor) and is cited as historically significant in television comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Influence on subsequent television programs, films, and plays is presented as a metric of the show's importance and impact on the comedy genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception, ratings, and critical recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Peak Nielsen ratings are listed (e.g., #4 in 1950–51) and the show appears on multiple 'best-of' lists (TV Guide, Time, Entertainment Weekly, Writers Guild of America).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popularity (ratings) and later critical rankings/awards are used as evaluative criteria for the show's success and standing among greatest TV shows. Specific placements (e.g., #30 on TV Guide's 50 Greatest TV Shows, #10 on Entertainment Weekly’s Top 100) are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notable guest appearances and star-driven draw
rubrics_metrics.description: The series featured guest performers such as José Ferrer and maintained a lineup of stars and specialty performers (baritone Jack Russell, Marguerite Piazza, the Hamilton Trio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of high-profile guests and specialty performers is discussed as contributing to the show's variety and appeal, and thus can be considered a criterion for programming quality.
